items.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: And it’s the same with Joe Farnsworth and John Webber, and those are the first people I call. Because I know we could fly 36 hours to some remote spot... and we could go up on stage and we don’t have even a talk through. I can just start playing something and they’re going to be right there.

ctx.x: And where or when does the decision come, like you decided to have the saxophone and the bass in unison.

We may have just decided that in the studio. You know a lot of times you show up at a recording session with a very skeletal arrangement or idea of what you’re going to do, or it’s a sketch of a tune and you just kind of throw ideas around the room and everyone just pipes up with their suggestion or their criticism and after a few minutes something clicks and everyone says okay that’ll work. But people kind of have to leave their egos at the door to do that. You know you can’t come in with this idea this is how I…
idea and it made it so easy to play. And it felt like our arrangement, our individual twist on it. So you have to listen to the musicians.
